title: Composite Systems and Tensor Products
intro: Two quantum systems together are described by the tensor product of their state spaces, so $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes. This page fixes the conventions (basis order, which factor is which qubit) that every reservoir simulation relies on.

blocks.text: If qubit 1 is in $\vert a\rangle$ and qubit 2 in $\vert b\rangle$, the pair is in $\vert a\rangle\otimes\vert b\rangle$, written $\vert ab\rangle$. Numerically this is the Kronecker product of the two vectors. The basis of two qubits is $\vert00\rangle, \vert01\rangle, \vert10\rangle, \vert11\rangle$, in that order: the index of $\vert b_1b_2\cdots b_n\rangle$ is the binary number $b_1b_2\cdots b_n$, with qubit 1 as the most significant bit. That is the convention of `np.kron` with qubit 1 as the leftmost factor, and of every sample on the QRC shelf.

A general two-qubit state is any unit vector in this four-dimensional space, $\sum_{ij} c_{ij}\vert ij\rangle$. Only some of them are products $\vert a\rangle\otimes\vert b\rangle$; the rest are entangled (Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement)). A quick test: arrange the amplitudes into the $2\times2$ matrix $c_{ij}$. The state is a product exactly when that matrix has rank 1.

blocks.alt: Four boxes labelled |00>, |01>, |10>, |11> with indices 0 to 3 and the values of qubit 1 and qubit 2 under each; a note says the left Kronecker factor varies slowest and X on qubit 1 swaps indices 0 and 2, and 1 and 3.
blocks.caption: The basis order used by every simulator on the site: qubit 1 is the left factor and the most significant bit.

blocks.text: Operators on part of a system

An operator $A$ acting on qubit $i$ alone is $I\otimes\cdots\otimes A\otimes\cdots\otimes I$, with $A$ in slot $i$. The QRC samples build this with a small `op(o, i, n)` helper. Operators on different qubits commute. A two-qubit coupling such as $X_iX_j$ is the product of two such single-qubit operators. A Pauli string is a tensor product of one Pauli (or $I$) per qubit; there are $4^n$ of them and they form an orthogonal basis for all operators on $n$ qubits, which is why a density matrix of $n$ qubits has $4^n - 1$ real coordinates.
Exponential growth, and what it does and does not mean

blocks.caption: n qubits: 2ⁿ complex amplitudes, 4ⁿ density-matrix entries.

blocks.text: Thirty qubits need about a billion amplitudes; fifty are beyond any classical memory. This is the headline argument for quantum computing and quantum reservoirs. But a quantum device does not hand you those amplitudes: you learn about the state only through measurement, a few numbers at a time, each from many shots. The QRC shelf's Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability) is about exactly this gap between the size of the state and the size of what can be read from it.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
# Two qubits: basis order |00>, |01>, |10>, |11> with the LEFT factor as qubit 1
zero, one = np.array([1., 0]), np.array([0., 1])
print("|0>(x)|1> =", np.kron(zero, one), " (index 1 = binary 01)")
# Operators on one qubit act as A (x) I; ordering matters
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); I = np.eye(2)
v = np.kron(zero, zero)
print("X on qubit 1:", np.kron(X, I) @ v, "  X on qubit 2:", np.kron(I, X) @ v)
# A state is a product exactly when its 2x2 amplitude matrix has rank 1
def schmidt_rank(psi): return np.linalg.matrix_rank(psi.reshape(2, 2), tol=1e-12)
prod = np.kron([0.6, 0.8], [1 / np.sqrt(2), 1j / np.sqrt(2)])
bell = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1]) / np.sqrt(2)
print("rank of a product state:", schmidt_rank(prod), "   rank of the Bell state:", schmidt_rank(bell))
# Dimension count
for n in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20):
    print(f"n = {n:2d} qubits: state vector {2**n:>8d} amplitudes, density matrix {4**n:>14d} entries")

blocks.text: Output of the run: $\vert0\rangle\otimes\vert1\rangle$ is the basis vector at index 1 (binary 01). $X$ on qubit 1 sends $\vert00\rangle$ to index 2 ($\vert10\rangle$); $X$ on qubit 2 sends it to index 1 ($\vert01\rangle$). The amplitude matrix of a product state has rank 1 and that of the Bell state rank 2. The table shows 32 amplitudes and 1024 density-matrix entries at 5 qubits, and about $10^{12}$ entries at 20.

blocks.title: Index of a basis state
blocks.text: At which index (counting from 0) is $\vert1\rangle\otimes\vert0\rangle\otimes\vert1\rangle$ in the 8-dimensional vector of three qubits?
solution: Read the bits as a binary number with qubit 1 first: $101_2 = 5$.

blocks.title: Product or entangled
blocks.text: Is $\tfrac12(\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle + \vert10\rangle + \vert11\rangle)$ a product state? If so, of what?
solution: All four amplitudes are $\tfrac12$, so the amplitude matrix has two equal rows: rank 1, a product.

blocks.title: Counting operators
blocks.text: How many Pauli strings act on 3 qubits, and how many of them are diagonal in the computational basis?
solution: Each qubit carries one of $I, X, Y, Z$: $4^3 = 64$ strings.
Diagonal ones use only $I$ and $Z$: $2^3 = 8$, including the identity.
